name: Shimshai
source_summary: A Persian government scribe who, with the commander Rehum, wrote to King Artaxerxes accusing the returned Jews of rebellion and successfully halted the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls for a time.
family_friendly_summary: After some Jewish exiles returned to Jerusalem, they began rebuilding the city walls. Not everyone was happy about this. A government scribe named Shimshai worked with an official named Rehum to write a letter to the Persian king, accusing the Jews of planning to rebel if the walls went up. Their plan worked for a while -- the king ordered the building to stop, and Shimshai and his officials hurried to Jerusalem and forced the workers to stop by force. Later, though, a different king allowed the work to continue and it was finished anyway. Shimshai's story shows that human opposition cannot permanently stop what God has planned.
adult_story: Shimshai was a Persian government scribe stationed in Samaria who, together with the commander Rehum and other officials, opposed the Jewish rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls during the reign of Artaxerxes. Shimshai co-authored a letter to the king warning that if the "rebellious and evil city" were rebuilt, its inhabitants would refuse to pay tribute and Persian control of the region would suffer (Ezra 4:8-16). The letter worked: Artaxerxes, after having the royal records searched, ordered the work stopped until further notice (4:17-22). Ezra records that once the decree reached Rehum, Shimshai, and their associates, "they went in haste to Jerusalem... and stopped them by force and power," halting construction (4:23). Shimshai's opposition was real and effective in the moment, but it was not the end of the story -- the narrative that follows in Ezra 5-6 shows the temple work resuming and eventually the walls themselves being finished under Nehemiah despite continued hostility from surrounding officials. Shimshai's brief, self-interested appearance in the text stands as one instance of a recurring biblical pattern: earthly powers can delay God's purposes for His people for a season, but Scripture consistently shows those purposes ultimately accomplished.
